question: What is the main goal of community mobilisation?

options.A: Empowering people to take action on their own health issues
options.B: Handing down medical instructions from government officials
options.C: Building large hospitals in rural and urban areas
options.D: Providing free prescription drugs to every household

explanation: Community mobilisation focuses on enabling local populations to identify and solve their own health challenges rather than relying entirely on outside help. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h1)

question: Why is community ownership critical for the success of a health project?

options.A: It ensures the community will sustain the project after external aid ends
options.B: It removes the need for any financial planning or budgeting
options.C: It guarantees that no one in the village will ever fall sick again
options.D: It allows nurses to stop visiting the community entirely

explanation: When people own a project, they care for it and keep it running long after outside organisations leave. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h1)

question: Which principle ensures that vulnerable voices are heard equally during community meetings?
explanation: Equity focuses on fairness and making sure that everyone, especially the less powerful, gets a chance to speak and participate. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h2)

question: What is the main danger of health workers assuming they know what the community needs best?

options.A: It leads to interventions that the community rejects or ignores
options.B: It causes the government to spend too much money on drugs
options.C: It forces local leaders to step down from their positions
options.D: It immediately stops all outbreaks of infectious diseases

explanation: Ignoring local input results in programs that do not fit the people's actual lifestyle or priorities, leading to failure. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of community entry in the mobilisation cycle?

options.A: Collecting taxes from local market traders
options.B: Building a permanent health clinic building
options.C: Conducting mass vaccinations for all children
options.D: Gaining social and legal acceptance from local leaders

explanation: Community entry is all about introducing yourself, getting permission, and building trust with local leaders before starting any work. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h3)

question: A nurse arrives in a new village to start a malaria project. What should she do FIRST?

options.A: Order the demolition of stagnant water pools near the houses
options.B: Distribute mosquito nets to the first people she meets on the road
options.C: Set up a treatment table in the market square and wait for patients
options.D: Visit the village chief and key community leaders to introduce herself

explanation: Proper community entry requires meeting leadership and building rapport before taking any health action. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h3)

question: What is a community diagnosis?

options.A: A laboratory test used to confirm typhoid fever
options.B: A prescription written for a patient with severe malaria
options.C: An official report written by the Minister of Health
options.D: An assessment of the overall health status of a population

explanation: A community diagnosis looks broadly at the health, living conditions, and resources of an entire group of people. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h4)

question: What is the difference between a felt need and a real need?

options.A: A felt need is what people ask for, while a real need is proven by health data
options.B: A felt need costs money, while a real need is completely free
options.C: A felt need is decided by the nurse, while a real need is ignored
options.D: A felt need only applies to children, while a real need applies to adults

explanation: Communities might express a desire for one thing based on perception, while data reveals a different underlying health priority. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h4)

question: Why is priority setting necessary during community mobilisation?

options.A: Resources are limited, so the community must focus on the most pressing problem
options.B: It stops people from talking during community meetings
options.C: Nurses are not allowed to work on more than two diseases at a time
options.D: The government requires every village to solve exactly one problem per year

explanation: Because time, money, and materials are limited, communities must rank their problems and tackle the most urgent ones first. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h5)

question: What should be included in a good community action plan?

options.A: An order for expensive medical equipment from foreign countries
options.B: A legal contract signed by every adult living in the district
options.C: A strict list of punishments for people who refuse to participate
options.D: Clear details on who will do what, when, and with what materials

explanation: An effective plan outlines specific roles, timelines, and resources so everyone knows their responsibilities. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h5)

question: What happens during the action and implementation phase?

options.A: A new set of leaders is elected to replace the old chiefs
options.B: The community votes to cancel the project due to high costs
options.C: Health workers sit in an office and write final reports
options.D: The plans created by the community are put into actual practice

explanation: Implementation is the doing phase where the agreed-upon activities, like clearing brush or building facilities, are carried out. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical role of the nurse during the implementation phase?

options.A: Motivating volunteers when the work gets difficult
options.C: Acting as a strict dictator who punishes lazy workers
options.D: Providing technical advice on health procedures

explanation: Nurses act as facilitators, advisors, and motivators, not as authoritarian bosses who punish community members. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h6)

question: What is the difference between monitoring and evaluation?

options.A: Monitoring is done by the government, while evaluation is done by children
options.B: Monitoring costs money, while evaluation is completely free
options.C: Monitoring happens continuously during the project, while evaluation measures final results
options.D: Monitoring focuses on drugs, while evaluation focuses on buildings

explanation: Monitoring tracks progress day-by-day, whereas evaluation looks back at the end to see if the main goals were met. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h7)

question: How do you know a health project has achieved sustainability?

options.A: The community can maintain the results and manage repairs without outside help
options.B: The foreign donors promise to keep sending money for the next ten years
options.C: The government takes over all financial responsibility for the village
options.D: The local nurse decides to stay in the village permanently

explanation: Sustainability means the local people have the skills, money, and will to keep the benefits going on their own. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h7)

question: What is a major error a nurse can make during community mobilisation?

options.A: Asking local leaders for permission to enter the village
options.B: Taking over leadership and making decisions for the community
options.C: Teaching mothers how to prepare oral rehydration salt
options.D: Working with local volunteers to clean up the environment

explanation: Nurses should facilitate and empower, not take control and rob the community of their self-reliance. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h8)

question: What is the ultimate aim of a community health nurse in mobilisation?

options.A: Building local capacity so the community runs its own health programs
options.B: Collecting data to publish research papers in medical journals
options.C: Making sure the local clinic receives a large budget from abroad
options.D: Ensuring the nurse becomes the most respected person in the village

explanation: The goal of community mobilisation is self-reliance, where locals have the skills to manage their health without constant outside intervention. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T6#GNS124_U4_T6_h8)
